name: Bettys
label: Bettys Tea Rooms
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Helen's Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'St Helen's Square' (way/646968968): middle (74 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N1503590443 (Betty's): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous tea room on St Helen's Square.

text.description:
Bettys is the tea room on the corner of St Helen's Square in the middle of York, and the square is where most visitors photograph it from. The corner window and the front of the building make a tidy subject, and the open space in front gives you room to step back and fit it all in. From some angles Mansion House appears behind, which helps show that this is a proper city-centre square rather than just a shopfront.

The usual picture is taken from across the square, looking towards the corner frontage. Stand far enough back that the whole corner sits in the frame with a little square in front of it. People tend to walk through the foreground, so take a few shots and pick the one with the cleanest gap. Queues can form along the front and around the side of the building at busy times, and they can block the view. If so, wait a minute or try a slightly different spot along the square.

It also works well after dark, when the corner window can be a feature of the picture. A 360-degree evening panorama has been taken here to capture it. Keep your phone upright for the facade, or turn it sideways if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. Please keep the doorway clear for people queuing.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of York, on St Helen's Square, with Mansion House visible from some angles across the square.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for St Helen's Square in the centre of York. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner window and facade. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to include more of the square. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a closer view of the window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Helen's Square (across the square from the Bettys corner frontage). The Bettys corner window and facade on St Helen's Square, with the square in front and Mansion House visible in the background from some angles. From here you see the corner window and facade with the square in front, and sometimes Mansion House in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the corner of the building on one of the vertical lines so it looks straight. Leave a band of open square at the bottom of the frame. Keep the phone level, because tilting it makes the building lean. If the queue is in the way, wait for a gap or take a closer shot of the window with telephoto instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the window or sky looks too bright. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body. For a wider view of the square, try panorama mode and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Queues can build up at busy times and may block the view, so be ready to wait for a gap. In the evening the lit window can look good, so try a night-mode shot or a panorama then.

text.access_note: St Helen's Square is open public space, but Bettys is a business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: The Shambles
label: The Shambles
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Shambles' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23693559: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Shambles' (122 m long).
notes: Narrow medieval street with overhanging timber-framed houses.

text.description: The Shambles is a narrow lane in the middle of York, and it is probably the most photographed street in the city. Timber-framed houses lean towards each other, their upper floors jutting out over the cobbles by several feet, so the sky shrinks to a thin strip. That gives a phone photo strong lines and a lot of depth. Many of the buildings date from roughly 1350 to 1475, which means the street keeps a large amount of original medieval building fabric. The name comes from an Old English word for a butcher's bench or stall. In 1885 there were thirty-one butchers' shops here, and the last closed in the early twentieth century. Look for the meat hooks still hanging outside some shopfronts, with shelves below them. They make good close-up details. The tall, close buildings shade the street, so the light is soft and even rather than harsh. The street is at its busiest from mid-morning to late afternoon in summer, so for a clear view of the lane, go before 9am or after dark. Stand at the phone icon on the map and look south down the lane, so the leaning buildings close in on both sides and lead the eye away from you. The cobbles are uneven, so watch your footing while you hold up your phone.
text.geographic_location: The Shambles is in the historic centre of York, running between Newgate at the north end and Pavement at the south end. King's Square is nearby.
text.directions_text: Start from the city centre around King's Square, Newgate or Pavement and walk to the middle of the street. The phone icon on the map is slightly north of where Little Shambles used to join the street. Walk to it and turn to face south. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the lane much as your eye sees it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds or the narrow street stop you from stepping back, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, more compressed view of the leaning upper floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the narrow lane running away from you, with the overhanging timber-framed upper storeys closing in on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the lane in the centre, with the vertical lines of the buildings straight against the grid so they don't tilt. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level, which also stops the buildings leaning backwards. If hanging signs and awnings cross the frame, shift a step to one side until you find a cleaner line. For a wider view of the whole crooked row of buildings, try King's Square, from a distance rather than inside the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the street itself to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright strip of sky doesn't turn white. Use night mode after dark, and hold your phone against a wall or your own chest to keep it steady. Live Photos can be handy for catching a moment when people have cleared from the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9am, when the street is least crowded. Several guides also suggest after dark.

text.access_note: The Shambles is an open public street that can be visited at any time, though the cobbles are uneven; check the official site before you go for anything about the shops along it.
claims_not_in_sources: Tall buildings on both sides mean the light in the lane is soft and shaded rather than harsh.
The position slightly north of where Little Shambles used to join the street is where guides suggest standing, looking south, for the best-known view.
The street is busiest from mid-morning to late afternoon in summer, and quieter before 9am or after dark.
Hanging signs and shopfront awnings can cross the frame in some positions along the lane.

name: York Minster
label: York Minster
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Minster Yard' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Minster Yard' (way/4486738): middle (103 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28750371: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'York Minster' (186 m across).
notes: Gothic cathedral and York's best-known landmark.

text.description:
York Minster is the great Gothic cathedral at the heart of York, and it is the seat of the Archbishop of York. The first church on the site was recorded in 627, but most of the building you see today went up between 1220 and 1472, with the two western towers added between 1433 and 1472. It is a Grade I listed building. It also keeps most of its medieval stained glass, including an east window said to be the largest expanse of medieval glass in the world.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is the west front from Minster Yard, the open ground by the main entrance. From here the twin towers and the carved doorways fit into one frame, and the building's full width is easier to show than from the side streets. It is a busy spot in the middle of the day, so early morning or early evening is the easier time, and the low light also picks out the stonework. If you want a different feel, Duncombe Place gives a straight-on view of the west front at the end of the street. Precentor's Court gives a quieter, closer view of the towers framed by old houses.

The Minster is still a working church, so stay out of the way of people going in and out, and keep your voice and movements considerate while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: York Minster stands in the historic centre of York, in the part of the city around Minster Yard and Duncombe Place. The cathedral fills the middle of its surrounding precinct.
text.directions_text: The classic west-front view from Minster Yard is a short walk round the building from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole west front and both towers in at close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved doorways and tower tops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Minster Yard (front of the west façade, by the main entrance). The full west front with its twin towers and detailed entrances, framed from the open ground in front of the cathedral. For the well-known west-front view with its twin towers and detailed entrances, walk a short way round the building to Minster Yard, where the open ground in front of the cathedral gives you room to frame it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep the phone level, and step back as far as the open ground allows so you do not have to tilt it upwards. For a variation, try Duncombe Place for the building filling the view at the end of the street. Shoot from the pavement or wait for a gap in the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the detail. Take a wide shot and a zoomed shot of the same view, as the carving looks very different close up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or early evening, when the light is low and there are fewer people. Guides differ on the best time, so check conditions on the day.

text.access_note: Some parts of the Minster precinct may restrict tripods during busy periods, and the Minster is a working church, so be considerate. The area in front is open public ground.
claims_not_in_sources: Minster Yard and Duncombe Place are busy with visitors during the day.
Duncombe Place has traffic, so it is safer to shoot from the pavement or wait for a gap.
Holding the phone level and using gridlines helps stop tall buildings looking as though they lean backwards.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail when a pale sky is in the frame.

name: National Railway Museum
label: Railway Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14999691: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Railway Museum' (511 m across).

text.description:
The National Railway Museum tells the story of Britain's railways and sits on the site of the old York North locomotive depot, where it has been since 1975. It is part of the Science Museum Group and holds the national collection of historic railway vehicles. Well-known names include Mallard, Flying Scotsman and Duchess of Hamilton, and there is also the leading vehicle of a Japanese 0 Series Shinkansen bullet train, one of only two Shinkansen vehicles shown outside Japan. More than 6,000 objects are on display, with around 100 locomotives or items of rolling stock at York at any one time.

It photographs well because the subjects are big, colourful and close together. Long steam engines, royal saloons and the historic Station Hall building give you strong lines and plenty of detail. The Station Hall is a Grade II listed former goods station from 1875-77. It reopened in 2025 after a major refurbishment, so the building itself is worth a frame as well as what stands inside it.

On your phone, start with a wide view to show the scale of an engine, then move in on the details: nameplates, wheels, brass and paintwork. Keep your phone steady and clean the lens before you start. Museum displays change from time to time, so a locomotive you have seen in older photos may have moved. Check the official site before you go for what is open and what is on display.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on Leeman Road in York, close to York railway station.
text.directions_text: The museum is within walking distance of York railway station, on Leeman Road. In summer months and school holidays a roadtrain runs to the museum from the city centre, near York Minster, and the York park and ride also serves it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for whole locomotives and big halls, and the default lens (1x) for general views. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as nameplates, badges and cab fittings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick an engine or hall that catches your eye and walk around it. Step back for the full length of a locomotive, then come in close for the details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the long lines of the engines straight. Shoot along the length of a locomotive from a front corner to give a sense of depth. Keep other visitors small in the frame to show the scale. Look for reflections in glass and avoid them by moving a little to one side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the engine to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if bright windows or lights wash out the picture. Indoors, hold the phone steady against your body or a rail. If your phone switches on night mode, wait for the shot to finish before you move.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day if you can, as there tend to be fewer people in your shots. Indoor light stays fairly constant, so the time matters less than the crowds.

text.access_note: This is a museum, so entry arrangements, opening days and which areas you can photograph may vary: check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Museum displays change from time to time, so a particular locomotive may have been moved.
Earlier in the day there are tend to be fewer visitors in the shots.
Reflections in glass cases can spoil photographs, and moving to one side can reduce them.
Phone night mode can need a steady hand for a second or two while it takes the picture.

name: Jorvik Viking Centre
label: Jorvik Viking Centre
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/316106165: the OpenStreetMap point 'Jorvik Viking Centre'.

text.description:
Jorvik Viking Centre is in York, on the site where archaeologists dug up the remains of the Viking city of Jórvík. It was created by York Archaeological Trust and opened in 1984. Inside, visitors ride through a recreated Viking settlement in 'time capsule' carriages, past lifelike figures and life-size scenes. Beyond the ride there is a museum area showing some 800 finds from the dig. The digs between 1976 and 1981 turned up well-preserved timber buildings, workshops and everyday objects, over 40,000 in all. By October 2022 the centre had welcomed 20 million visitors.

For a phone photographer, the appeal is the street outside the entrance, where the old name and the Viking story are part of the setting. Take a wide shot that includes the entrance and the people passing, then step in for a closer one of any signs or details that tell you where you are. Inside, rules on photography can differ from place to place and exhibit to exhibit, so look for signs and ask staff before you take pictures. The ride is dim and moving, so expect soft, blurry results there; the outside of the building will give you your sharpest, most reliable pictures. Keep the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames in case people walk through.
text.geographic_location: Jorvik Viking Centre is in York, on the Coppergate site, where the Coppergate Shopping Centre now stands.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of York and head to the Coppergate area, where the centre stands. The centre can be reached on foot from central York. The phone icon on the map is at the centre itself, so once you arrive you are already in position. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the entrance and street scene. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is tight and you want the whole frontage in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the entrance along one of the vertical lines. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean, and let a few passers-by into the frame to give a sense of scale. Then use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a sign or a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the entrance to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not turn dark. Take several frames, as people will keep walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people in the street, which makes a cleaner picture of the frontage. Overcast or soft light is kind to the building.

text.access_note: Jorvik Viking Centre is a visitor attraction, so entry and any photography rules inside may be ticketed or restricted; check the official site before you go.

name: Clifford's Tower
label: Clifford's Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tower Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Tower Gardens' (node/10212410017): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2755833: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Clifford's Tower' (35 m across).
notes: Norman keep on a grassy mound.

text.description:
Clifford's Tower is the ruined stone keep of York's medieval castle. It sits on a grassy mound and is one of the easiest buildings in the city to recognise. The first castle here was a wooden one, built on the orders of William the Conqueror in 1068. Henry III rebuilt the keep in stone in the middle of the 13th century, with an unusual quatrefoil (four-lobed) plan. An explosion in 1684 destroyed the interior, which is why it is a shell today. It is now looked after by English Heritage.

It photographs well because the mound lifts the tower clear of its surroundings, so you get a clean outline against the sky. From the lawns you can fit the tower, the River Ouse and the nearby obelisk into one frame, which gives you two buildings and some water in a single shot. The tower is a short stroll to the north-east, so you can walk up for a closer look afterwards.

For a different picture, the open ground of the Eye of York shows the tower from ground level, and the quatrefoil shape stands out against the sky. If you pay for the roof deck, you get a wide view over York's rooftops towards York Minster, with the tower's own roof as foreground. Check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of York, on its mound beside the former castle area and the York Castle Museum, close to the River Ouse and the Tower Gardens lawns.
text.directions_text: From the centre of York, head on foot for Tower Gardens beside the River Ouse. The mound is easy to spot as you approach. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower, the lawn and the obelisk together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more river and lawn around it, and to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tight shot of the tower on its mound.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tower Gardens. The tower rising from its grassy mound across the lawns, with the River Ouse and the obelisk nearby in the frame. In Tower Gardens, on the lawns beneath the tower. From here the tower rises from its grassy mound to the north-east, with the River Ouse and the obelisk close by in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the tower on one of the upper third points, with the lawn filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the obelisk as a second subject to one side. For a ground-level alternative, the Eye of York shows the quatrefoil shape against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework doesn't wash out. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean at the edges, especially at 0.5x.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer light early or late in the day suits stonework.

text.access_note: Tower Gardens and the base of the mound are free to reach, but going up the tower to the roof deck is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer light early or late in the day suits stonework.
Keeping the phone level reduces leaning walls, especially with the ultra-wide lens.

name: York City Walls
label: City Walls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Station Road' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Station Road and Station Rise (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18937491: large area 'York City Walls' (1923 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Medieval walls you can walk along.

text.description:
York's city walls make a ring of medieval stone around the old centre, and they are the longest town walls in England. York also has more miles of intact wall than any other English city. The walls are generally about 4 m high and 1.8 m wide, and you can walk along much of the top. The first defences here date from around 71 AD, when the Romans built a fort beside the River Ouse. Despite the nickname "Roman walls", most of the stonework you see today dates from the 13th to 14th centuries. The Victorians later repaired the walls and widened the wall-walk, including in the northern stretch with views of the cathedral. The walls are now a scheduled monument and a grade I listed structure.

They photograph well because the grey battlements give you a strong foreground line, with the rooftops and York Minster's towers behind. The best-known spot is on Station Road, at the steps up to the wall walk. From there a stretch of wall fills the foreground and the Minster's towers rise above the roofs. Use the wall as a leading line and keep the towers in the upper part of the frame. If you have time for a second view, Lendal Bridge shows the wall line running over the river approach, with Lendal Tower and the Minster beyond. The Multangular Tower is good for a close-up of the old stonework.

Take care on the wall-walk itself, as some sections have no inner railings. Keep one hand free and don't step backwards while framing a shot.
text.geographic_location: The walls encircle the medieval city centre of York.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of York and head north-west towards Station Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the wall and the Minster's towers in one frame. Then switch to the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the towers above the roofs. Use the default lens (1x) for a balanced view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Station Road and Station Rise (at the steps and platform up to the wall walk). A stretch of the walls in the foreground with York Minster's towers rising above the rooftops behind. Stand on Station Road, at the steps and platform up to the wall walk. From here the photo shows a stretch of the walls in the foreground, with York Minster's towers rising above the rooftops behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the wall along the lower third, so it leads the eye towards the Minster. Keep the phone level so the battlements don't slope. For a different view, try Lendal Bridge, where the wall line runs over the river approach with Lendal Tower and the Minster in the distance. The Multangular Tower is good for close-ups of the old stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Minster's towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework doesn't turn too dark. At dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against the wall to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, which one guide recommends for this spot.

text.access_note: The walls are free to walk, but they close at dusk, some sections have no inner railings, dogs are not allowed apart from assistance dogs, and parts may close for repairs, snow or ice, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit both the wall and the Minster's towers in one frame.
Bracing your elbows against the wall helps keep a night-mode shot steady.

name: York Castle Museum
label: York Castle Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1125235305: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'York Castle Museum' (166 m across).
notes: Museum in the former prison buildings.

text.description:
York Castle Museum sits on the site of York Castle, which William the Conqueror first built in 1068. The museum itself is much younger. It opened in 1938 and fills two old prison buildings: the Debtors' Prison, built in 1701–05 with stone from the ruined castle, and the Female Prison, built in the 1780s. The pale, formal frontages, the clock turret on the Debtors' Prison and the open space between the buildings make good, straightforward photographs. They also give you a real sense of how the site has changed over the centuries.

The museum is best known for Kirkgate, a recreated Victorian street. It was the first of its kind in Britain. The Debtors' Prison cells are also part of the visit, and Dick Turpin was held there in the 1730s. The museum sits just south of Clifford's Tower, so you can take in both on the same short walk.

For your phone, begin with a wide view of a whole building from a little way back, then move in for smaller details such as the clock turret, doorways and stonework. The museum site is about 166 m across, so walk around a bit rather than shooting everything from one spot. Check the official site before you go to see which parts are open and whether photography is allowed inside.
text.geographic_location: In York, on the site of the old York Castle. It stands immediately south of Clifford's Tower, with the castle wall and the River Foss beyond it to the south.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Clifford's Tower; the museum is immediately to the south of it, inside the former castle grounds. Once there, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the museum site. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of the buildings. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to a long frontage and cannot step back. Use the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the clock turret, doorways and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk a little way across the open space between the old prison buildings until one frontage fills your view, then take your photo from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the building with them so the walls look straight. Include a little of the open ground in front for scale. Then step in and take a tighter shot of one feature, such as the clock turret on the Debtors' Prison.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and the stone looks washed out. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the walls lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the stonework than harsh midday sun. Earlier in the day it is often easier to get a shot without many people in it.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum, and some parts may be closed at times, so check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and photography rules inside.

name: Yorkshire Museum
label: Yorkshire Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum Gardens' (relation/3600440): middle (406 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/13063082814: the OpenStreetMap point 'Yorkshire Museum'.
notes: Museum set in the Museum Gardens.

text.description:
The Yorkshire Museum sits in the Museum Gardens, with the ruins of St Mary's Abbey nearby, so you get a grand old building and a ruined abbey in one visit. The museum was designed by William Wilkins in a Greek Revival style and is Grade I listed. It opened in 1830, which makes it one of the longest-established museums in England. The land was granted to the Yorkshire Philosophical Society from the former St Mary's Abbey estate, on condition that the grounds around the museum became botanic gardens. Those gardens are now the Museum Gardens.

The best phone photo here is a person or selfie shot with the abbey ruins in the background, taken from the gardens wherever the ruins are in view. This is the pose the York selfie trail suggests, and it works because the ruins give a strong, old-stone backdrop. Walk about 90 m east towards the museum and you can frame the museum's exterior filling the picture instead. The gardens are free to enter, so you can take both shots without going inside the museum.

Go in late afternoon for warm light, or early in the morning if you want it quieter. If you do visit the museum itself, look for signs about photography, because rules can change and flash may not be allowed. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
text.geographic_location: The Yorkshire Museum stands in the Museum Gardens in York, on land that once belonged to St Mary's Abbey. The abbey ruins are in the gardens nearby.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon around golden hour is the suggested time. Early morning is also worth trying.

name: Merchant Adventurers' Hall, York
label: Merchant Adventurers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piccadilly' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Piccadilly nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W138371703 (Merchant Adventurers' Hall): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Merchant Adventurers' Hall stands in the middle of York, and its best-known side is the one that faces the river. From there you can see the timber-framed upper storey and the brick chapel together, with the garden and the riverside in front. Guides describe this as the better-known face of the building, and the view across the garden is the one most often painted and photographed. That mix of old timber, brick and greenery gives you layers to work with, so even a quick phone shot has depth.

Face the Hall and let the garden fill the lower part of the picture, with the timber storey and chapel above it. If you want a second picture, walk to Fossgate. From there the ceremonial gatehouse entrance is framed by the street, with a coat of arms above the doorway. It makes a very different photograph from the garden view, and Fossgate is another recommended viewpoint for the Hall.

Fossgate is closed to cars for much of the day, so it is largely pedestrian and easier to stand and compose a shot. The walled garden and the interior are reached through the Hall, so check the official site before you go if you want to photograph inside.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of York, on the river side of the Hall, with Piccadilly opposite it and the gatehouse entrance on Fossgate.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Piccadilly in York city centre. From there the Hall is to the north-east, less than a minute on foot. For the gatehouse view, walk round to Fossgate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view of the Hall across its garden. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow or you want more of the garden and riverside. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the timber detail and the chapel brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Piccadilly (opposite the Hall, where the street opens onto the river side). The timber-framed upper storey and the brick chapel, with the garden and riverside in the foreground. Opposite the Hall, where the street opens onto the river side. From here you see the timber-framed upper storey and the brick chapel, with the garden and riverside in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the timber storey on the upper line and the garden on the lower one, so the building does not sit in the middle of the frame. Keep your phone upright so the verticals stay straight. For a second view, take the gatehouse entrance on Fossgate with its coat of arms above the doorway, and use the street to lead the eye towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the timber to focus. If the sky is bright and the building looks dark, drag the exposure slider down a little. Wait for people to move out of the foreground, or take a Live Photo and choose the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the light is soft, such as early morning or late afternoon, and when there are fewer people on the street.

text.access_note: The view from Piccadilly and Fossgate is from the street, but the walled garden and interior are reached through the Hall and may need an entry fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft early-morning or late-afternoon light and fewer people are usually better for photographs here.
Turning the phone upright helps keep the verticals of the building straight.

name: Micklegate Bar
label: Micklegate Bar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Blossom Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Blossom Street nearest the subject (our map tiles); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18937491: large area 'York City Walls' (1923 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Ceremonial southwest gate of the city.

text.description:
Micklegate Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', that interrupt York's city walls. In medieval times these gates restricted traffic and were used to collect tolls. Today the bar is part of a wall circuit that is a scheduled monument and a grade I listed structure, and York has more miles of intact wall than any other city in England. The Victorians restored much of the walls, including the battlements, so what you see is a mix of medieval work and later repair.

It photographs well because the gatehouse is a strong, simple shape: towers either side of a central arch, with the road running straight up to it. The best-known angle is head-on from Blossom Street, on the south side of the street, where the whole front of the gatehouse sits at the end of the road. From there you get the towers and the arch together, which is hard to manage from closer in. For a second picture, try the view along Micklegate, which shows the inner face of the bar with the street running through the arch.

Keep the bar centred and turn on your gridlines so the towers stay upright. Wait for a gap in the people and traffic before you shoot, and keep to the pavement while you frame the picture. Both viewpoints are on public streets, so there is nothing to pay to take the photo.
text.geographic_location: Micklegate Bar is one of the four main bars on York's city walls. Blossom Street and Micklegate are the two streets used for the viewpoints, and for the main view you stand on the south side of Blossom Street, facing the bar.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from York city centre and head towards Micklegate Bar and Blossom Street. Blossom Street is the street that leads up to the bar; stand on its south side facing the bar. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the head-on view of the whole gatehouse. If the road and buildings either side crowd the frame, a little zoom (2x) can tidy it up. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close, and keep the bar in the middle of the frame so the edges do not stretch it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Blossom Street (straight on, facing the bar from the south side of the street). The full front of the gatehouse, with its towers and arch, seen head-on from the street that leads up to it. From here the full front of the gatehouse, with its towers and arch, is seen head-on at the end of the street. For the alternative, walk through to Micklegate and shoot the inner face of the gatehouse with the street running through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the arch up with the centre line so the towers look level. Let the street lead the eye towards the gate, and leave a little space above the battlements. For a second shot, turn to Micklegate to frame the bar with the historic street around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the arch to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in for a sharp shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No particular time of day is firmly recommended for this view. Quieter moments help keep people and vehicles out of the frame. If you are here after dark and the bar is lit, try night mode and hold the phone still against a wall or post.

text.access_note: Both viewpoints are on public streets, but check the official site before you go if you plan to walk the wall itself.

name: Bootham Bar
label: Bootham Bar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Exhibition Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Exhibition Square' (relation/1791851): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18937491: large area 'York City Walls' (1923 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Bootham Bar is the gatehouse that forms one of the four main gateways, or 'bars', of York's city walls, which once controlled traffic and collected tolls. It photographs well because it is a compact stone gate with a dark arch, with red roofs and the towers of York Minster rising behind it. That combination says 'York' in a single frame. The walls here follow the line of the original Roman defences, which date from around 71 AD, though most of the stonework you see is medieval and Victorian restoration. The Victorians also widened the wall-walk on the northern stretch, which now has views of the Minster. The walls are a scheduled monument and a grade I listed building.

The classic view is from Exhibition Square, just outside the bar, by the William Etty statue. It is a popular spot, so expect other people to be taking the same photo. Take your time and wait for a gap in the pedestrians. Keep the arch roughly centred, let the Minster show above and behind it, and check that the gate's walls are not leaning in the frame. If you want a second angle, walk to High Petergate, where the gate is framed at the end of the street with the Minster beyond. You can also go up onto the walls for a view along Petergate. Take care with the traffic here: the Exhibition Square view needs a crossing of a busy road at the traffic lights.
text.geographic_location: Bootham Bar is one of the four main bars of York's city walls. Exhibition Square is outside the bar, and High Petergate leads to it with the gate framed at the end of the street. York Minster stands just behind it, inside the walls.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of York and walk to Bootham Bar on the city walls. Exhibition Square is the open space directly outside the gate. Use the traffic lights to cross the road safely. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate, the roofs and the Minster together. Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the Minster closer behind the arch. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are very close to the gate or want the whole square in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Exhibition Square (outside the bar, below the William Etty statue, on the right of the statue). The gate with its arch and the red roofs and York Minster rising behind it. The viewpoint to aim for is Exhibition Square, outside the bar, by the William Etty statue. From there the photo shows the gate with its arch, and the red roofs and York Minster rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch on the centre line so the gate sits straight. Hold the phone level, since tilting it will make the gate lean. Let the Minster rise above the top of the gate. For a second view, try High Petergate, with the gate framed at the end of the street and the Minster beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework of the gate to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and the roofs keep their colour and the dark arch does not wash out. If people keep walking through, take a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning and golden hour are recommended by photo guides. Mid-afternoon sun can be harsh on the stonework.

text.access_note: The square outside the gate is open public space, and the city walls are free to walk, but they may close at dusk, so check the official site on the day before you go.

name: St Mary's Abbey, York
label: St Mary's Abbey
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum Gardens' (relation/3600440): middle (406 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/57854218: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mary's Abbey' (138 m across).
notes: Ruined Benedictine abbey in the Museum Gardens.

text.description:
St Mary's Abbey is a ruined Benedictine abbey that now sits among the lawns and flower beds of Museum Gardens, on a sloping site just west of York Minster. A church was first founded here in 1055 and dedicated to Saint Olaf. It was refounded in 1088, and a grand new church was begun the following year. The tall arches and wall fragments you see today come from a rebuilding that started in 1271 and was finished by 1294. At full size that church was about 110 m long, which helps explain why even the surviving pieces feel so large. The abbey was closed in 1539 during the dissolution of the monasteries and much of it was destroyed afterwards. It is now a scheduled monument.

The ruins photograph well because pale stone arches stand against open sky with soft green lawns around them. From the classic angle, near the Museum Street entrance, the arches make a backdrop and the garden flowers fill the foreground. That gives you depth without any fuss. The gardens are free to enter, but they are busy in summer, so an early visit gives cleaner pictures with fewer people in the frame. Take the wide view first, then walk closer for details of the arches and doorways.
text.geographic_location: In Museum Gardens, in the centre of York, on the west side of York Minster and a short way from the River Ouse. The Museum Street entrance is just north of Lendal Bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of York near York Minster. The gardens lie to the west of the Minster. The Museum Street entrance, just north of Lendal Bridge, is the way in for the classic postcard angle. From there, the ruins are about 81 m to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit more of the arches and flowers in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the arches and doorways.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Museum Gardens (Museum Street entrance, just north of Lendal Bridge, looking across the lawns to the ruins). The abbey's arches and walls framed as a backdrop, with the gardens' flowers in the foreground. From here the abbey's arches and walls make the backdrop. For the classic postcard angle, which is a separate viewpoint near the Museum Street entrance just north of Lendal Bridge, the gardens' flowers fill the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the main arch on one of the lines, with the flowers along the bottom of the frame. Keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. For a different view, walk closer to the ruins for detail shots of the medieval arches and doorways with the gardens behind. You can also try the less-used side of the gardens for a quieter angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stone to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is washing out. Use the 0.5x lens only when you have room, and keep straight lines away from the edges of the frame, where they can stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early, especially in summer. The Museum Street entrance is the most used one, and earlier visits give emptier shots.

text.access_note: The ruins are inside Museum Gardens, which is free to enter, but check the official site for the gardens' opening times before you go.

name: Walmgate Bar
label: Walmgate Bar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lawrence Street corner' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Lawrence Street and Walmgate (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18937491: large area 'York City Walls' (1923 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Only city gate with a surviving barbican.

text.description:
Walmgate Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', that punctuate York's city walls. In medieval times these gates restricted traffic and were used to collect tolls. Walmgate Bar has an outer barbican and an archway with a portcullis, all of which can be seen from the road. The inner face has a later timber-framed Elizabethan extension and a coat of arms over the passage, which gives you two quite different pictures from one building. The walls around York are the longest town walls in England, and most of what you see today dates from the 13th to 14th centuries, with Victorian repairs. They are now a scheduled monument and a grade I listed structure.

It is a simple place to fit the whole gate into one frame. The bar sits at a busy junction, so traffic, road signs and parked cars can creep into the shot. Wait for a gap in the traffic and keep the phone level so the gate stands upright. For a second view, go up onto the walls route and look at the barbican from above and beside, where its outer defences are clearer. There is also a café in the gatehouse if you want a break.
text.geographic_location: Walmgate Bar is part of York's medieval walls, at the busy junction of Walmgate and Foss Islands Road. It is the gateway on the Walmgate side of the city.
text.directions_text: Walmgate Bar is at the junction of Walmgate and Foss Islands Road. Take care at the junction, as it is busy with traffic. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole barbican and archway. If a wall or pavement stops you stepping back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the gate in the middle of the frame so the edges don't stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the portcullis and the coat of arms.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Lawrence Street and Walmgate (corner by Jenny's Fish & Chips, looking west toward the bar). The gate's outer barbican and archway with portcullis, seen straight down the road from across the junction. From here the gate's outer barbican and the archway with its portcullis line up straight down the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the archway in the centre, with the barbican filling most of the frame. Keep the vertical lines of the walls straight, and crop out signs and parked cars where you can. For another view, take the walls route and photograph the barbican from above and beside, or capture the inner face with its Elizabethan timber-framed extension and the coat of arms over the passage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the archway to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out the stonework. Take a few shots in a row, as cars and people keep passing through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on the road and gives softer light, but the junction is busy at most times. Check how the light falls on the face of the gate when you arrive.

text.access_note: The bar stands in a public street, and the barbican can be walked through on the walls route using the steps either side of Walmgate; check the official site before you go for current access to the walls and the gatehouse café.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning light is likely to fall on the face of the gate when seen from the east, and the road is likely to be quieter early in the day.
Ultra-wide shots can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Treasurer's House, York
label: Treasurer's House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Minster Yard' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Minster Yard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/241061247: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Treasurer's House' (63 m across).

text.description: Treasurer's House is a Grade I listed historic house owned by the National Trust, on Minster Yard just north of York Minster. It photographs well because the symmetrical stone front and the entrance gate make a neat, balanced frame, with the Minster precinct around it. The first Treasurer of the Minster was appointed in 1091, though little of the original house survives. The Young family added the symmetrical front in the early 17th century, which is the look you see today. In 1930 the local industrialist Frank Green gave the house and its contents to the National Trust. The house was built over a Roman road, which is behind a well-known ghost story about marching Roman soldiers in the cellar. For the classic picture, stand on Minster Yard about 40 m south-west of the house and frame the gate and the house front together. If the garden is open, a second view shows the stone front rising behind the lawn, statues and clipped topiary, sometimes with the Minster towers above. The garden may not always be free to enter, so check garden access on the day, and treat the street view as your reliable fallback. On a phone, keep your lines straight with the gridlines on, and watch for passers-by walking through the gateway. Photography may be restricted inside the house, so ask at the door.
text.geographic_location: Treasurer's House is in the Minster precinct in the centre of York, on Minster Yard directly north of York Minster.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for York Minster, then look for the house directly to its north on Minster Yard. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the house front and gate together. If the street feels tight, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the house in the middle of the frame so the edges don't stretch. If you are in the garden, use telephoto (2x or more) for the stonework, statues and topiary.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Minster Yard (opposite the house's front gate, looking south-west). The Treasurer's House frontage and its entrance gate, with the Minster's cathedral precinct around it. From here the house and its entrance gate are to the north-east, with the Minster precinct around it. This is not exactly opposite the gate, so walk a little closer if you want a straighter view of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate with the centre of the house so the symmetry shows. Keep the phone level so the walls stay upright. If the garden is open, the view over the lawn to the stone front is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone front to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. Take a couple of frames in case someone walks through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is a good time for the sunlit house front. Earlier in the day also usually means fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The house is a National Trust property with an admission fee. The garden may not always be free, so check opening times and garden access on the official site on the day.

name: Stonegate
label: Stonegate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Helen's Square' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'St Helen's Square' (way/646968968): middle (74 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W4436828 (Stonegate): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic pedestrian street leading to the Minster.

text.description:
Stonegate is one of York's best-known streets for a photograph, and the reason is the view along it. Historic timber-fronted buildings line both sides, and at the far end York Minster rises above the rooftops. That gives you a ready-made picture with a foreground, a middle and a clear point of interest at the top.

The street is busy with visitors, so standing in the middle of it can mean people in every frame. A slightly calmer option is the edge of St Helen's Square, at the mouth of Stonegate. From there you look straight down the street towards the Minster, and you can take in the whole run of buildings without being jostled.

For a second angle, walk up towards the Minster and try Minster Yard. There the towers sit close above the buildings at the top of Stonegate, and the street leads down towards you.

Keep the phone level so the building fronts stay upright. Gridlines help with that. Wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or accept a few figures as a sense of scale. An early or late visit usually means fewer people. Check your lens and screen are clean before you start, because it is easy to take a dozen shots in the same spot and find them all smeared.
text.geographic_location: Stonegate is in the centre of York, running from St Helen's Square towards York Minster.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the centre of York and look for St Helen's Square. Stonegate leads off the square to the north-east, towards the Minster. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the full length of the street. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the Minster closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Helen's Square (from the square's edge at the mouth of Stonegate, looking down the street). A view straight down Stonegate with the Minster in the distance at the top of the street. At the edge where it meets the start of Stonegate, and look down the street. The Minster appears in the distance at the top of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the street so the buildings lead the eye towards the Minster, and use gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For a different angle, try Minster Yard at the top of the street, where the towers rise close above the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Minster to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take a few frames in a row so you can pick the one with the fewest people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the evening, when fewer people are likely to be in the street.

text.access_note: Stonegate is a public street; check conditions locally before you go, and check the official site if you plan to go into any building.

name: Lendal Bridge
label: Lendal Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ouse Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ouse Bridge' (way/4434556): middle (72 m across); moved 35 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/18953812: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'The Millennium Bridge' (148 m long).
notes: Iron bridge over the Ouse with Minster views.

text.description:
Lendal Bridge is a Victorian Gothic Revival bridge that carries traffic over the River Ouse at the point where York's city walls break for the river. It links two medieval towers, Lendal Tower on the east bank and Barker Tower on the west. The bridge was designed by Thomas Page, who also designed London's Westminster Bridge. It opened in 1863 and is made of cast iron, with a single span of about 53 m. It is Grade II listed. The first attempt at a bridge here, begun in 1860, collapsed during construction, and five workmen were killed. Before that, a rope ferry crossed at this spot.

The bridge is a poor subject from on top of it, because you are standing on the structure and it falls out of frame. A classic view is from Ouse Bridge. From there the bridge sits in the middle distance. The water fills the foreground, and the Guildhall and moored boats add interest at the sides. The river leads the eye along to the bridge, which makes a tidy composition for a phone. If you want a second angle, try Museum Gardens on the far bank, where the river and riverside buildings lead down to the bridge. Wait for a gap in the pedestrians and boats, and keep the phone level so the bridge does not look tilted.
text.geographic_location: Lendal Bridge crosses the River Ouse in central York, between the railway station side and the York Minster side of the city. The view described here is from Ouse Bridge, near the Guildhall.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from York city centre near the Guildhall and the river. Ouse Bridge is the road bridge over the Ouse there. Once on Ouse Bridge, look for Lendal Bridge, the Gothic-style bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the river, the bridge and the buildings beside it. Then try 2x or 3x to bring Lendal Bridge closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of water and sky, as it will make the bridge look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ouse Bridge (looking back up the river toward Lendal Bridge). The Victorian Gothic bridge in the middle distance, with the river in the foreground and the Guildhall and moored boats nearby. Where Lendal Bridge sits in the middle distance, with the river in front of you and the Guildhall and moored boats close by. Stand where the view works on the day, as the exact spot is up to you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge on a third, with the river running up the frame towards it. Keep the horizon level. Include some moored boats or the riverside buildings in the foreground to add depth. For a different angle, Museum Gardens gives a view down the river from the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework and ironwork keep their detail. At dusk, switch on night mode. Rest your elbows on the parapet and hold still while it captures.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or blue hour, when the river can reflect the bridge and the sky colour.

text.access_note: Ouse Bridge and the riverside are open public places, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or works.

name: Monk Bar
label: Monk Bar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Goodramgate' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Goodramgate nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18937491: large area 'York City Walls' (1923 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Monk Bar is one of the four main gatehouses, or 'bars', that interrupt York's city walls. Gatehouses like this once slowed traffic and were used to collect tolls. The walls around it are a scheduled monument and a grade I listed structure, and York has more miles of intact wall than any other city in England. Much of what you see today dates from the 13th and 14th centuries, tidied up by the Victorians, who widened the wall-walk and rebuilt many of the battlements.

The best view for a phone photo is from Goodramgate, on the city side of the walls. From the Goodramgate end you look straight at the inner face of the gatehouse, with its arches, shields and upper storeys. It is a tall, ornate building in a fairly narrow street, so you can show how it towers over everything around it. For a different view, go out through the gate to Monkgate and shoot the full front, with its big central arch and smaller side arches, straight on. Or climb the narrow, steep stone steps from Goodramgate to the wall-walk. From there you can photograph a stretch of medieval wall with York Minster rising over the rooftops, framed by the gatehouse behind you.

The streets here are busy, so check for people and traffic before you step back to frame a shot. The attraction inside the gate was closed when we last checked and may not reopen, so plan to enjoy Monk Bar from the outside.
text.geographic_location: Monk Bar is a gatehouse in York's city walls, seen from Goodramgate on the city side and from Monkgate on the outside.
text.directions_text: There are no listed railway or tram stops to start from, so begin in York city centre and head for Goodramgate on foot. Walk to the end of the street and you will find the gatehouse in front of you. Vehicle access around here is restricted, so expect to finish on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrow street to fit the whole gatehouse in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the shields and the details of the upper storeys.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Goodramgate (city-side (inside the walls), facing the gatehouse from the Goodramgate end). The inner face of Monk Bar's gatehouse with its arches, shields and upper storeys, seen from the street inside the walls. On the city side of the walls, facing the gatehouse from the Goodramgate end. Stay on the pavement and look out for traffic and other pedestrians.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the gatehouse centred, with the vertical lines of the building straight so it does not lean. Tilt the phone up as little as you can, or the tower will look as if it is falling backwards. For a second view, go through to Monkgate and shoot the full front straight on, or climb to the wall-walk for the wall with York Minster beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly, so the sky does not wash out the detail on the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide says the walls close at dusk, so go earlier in the day if you want to walk the wall; check the official opening times.

text.access_note: The gatehouse can be photographed from open public streets, but the wall-walk is reached by narrow, steep steps and may close at dusk, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean, and gridlines help keep verticals straight.
Lowering the exposure slightly can stop a bright sky washing out stonework detail.

name: Ouse Bridge, York
label: Ouse Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King's Staith' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'King's Staith' (way/548812612): middle (46 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/18953812: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'The Millennium Bridge' (148 m long).
notes: Historic crossing over the River Ouse, riverside quays nearby.

text.description: Ouse Bridge is a road bridge over the River Ouse in the middle of York, and the best view of it is from the riverbank rather than from the bridge itself. Seen from below, the wide central arch sits above the water, with the pub terrace and the river filling the foreground. That gives you a layered picture with something close, something in the middle and the bridge behind. There has been a bridge here for a very long time. The Vikings built a wooden one, which collapsed in 1154 under a crowd waiting to greet St William of York. A stone bridge followed in the later 12th century, and in 1367 it carried what were probably the first public toilets in England. Houses, shops, a chapel and a jail once stood on it, but they were taken down between 1745 and 1793. The bridge you see today was designed by Peter Atkinson the younger and finished in 1821. It is a Grade II listed building. For your photo, go down to the terrace by the water and turn to face the bridge. Keep the pub terrace and the river in the lower part of the frame, and let the arch fill the middle. If the river is high, take care, because the terrace can flood. Look at the ground before you go down, and stay back from the water's edge.
text.geographic_location: Ouse Bridge crosses the River Ouse in York city centre, between Lendal Bridge and Skeldergate Bridge. The viewpoint is on King's Staith, on the east (south-east) bank below the bridge, by the pub terrace.
text.directions_text: Head for Ouse Bridge in the city centre, then cross to the east side of the river and go down the steps to the pub terrace on King's Staith. Allow time to check the river level and the ground when you reach the steps. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the bridge from the terrace. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more terrace and water in the foreground, but keep the bridge away from the edges, where it can look stretched. A 2x telephoto, if your phone has one, is good for the arch and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on King's Staith (east (south-east) bank, below the bridge, by the pub terrace). The bridge spanning the river from the riverside, with the pub terrace and the water in the foreground. On the east (south-east) bank below the bridge, by the pub terrace. From here you look across the water to the bridge, with the terrace and the river in front of you. Do not use the bridge deck for this shot, because from there you look down the river rather than at the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge's arch on the upper third, with the water and terrace in the lower two thirds. Keep the horizon level. For a different angle, try Skeldergate Bridge, which looks back up the river to Ouse Bridge, or Lendal Bridge, which shows Ouse Bridge down the river with the Guildhall on the left.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo, which can catch boats or people moving past.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the stonework, and calm water gives the best reflections. Go when the river is low, as the terrace can flood when the Ouse rises.

text.access_note: The bridge and the riverside are public spaces, but the terrace can flood when the river is high, so check river levels and the ground before you go down.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits the stonework.
Calm water gives better reflections.
Wide-angle lenses can stretch subjects near the edges of the frame.
Ouse Bridge lies between Lendal Bridge and Skeldergate Bridge upstream and downstream (from the order of the bridges in the sources).
